title: Bede
hookLine: a monk who wrote a history of the English church and died finishing a translation

cards: "Dear master, there's still one sentence not written." A boy is sitting with a pen in a monk's cell in the north of England. On the floor nearby, an old monk is dying, short of breath.
They've been working all day, the old man dictating, the boy writing, and they're nearly done. All week, one man has stood behind the stories: Hilda, Caedmon, Cuthbert, Augustine and the temples.
This dying monk wrote them down. His name is Bede.

teach.b: Bede tells a little about himself at the end of his history of the English church. He was given to the monastery as a child and spent his whole life there, at Wearmouth and Jarrow.
His delight, he says, was always in learning, or teaching, or writing.
He wrote in Latin, the language of scholars, and he wrote a great deal: on scripture, on time and the calendar, on the saints, and the history this path has been reading from all week.
His death is told in a letter from one of his students, a monk named Cuthbert, not the Cuthbert of the otters.

In his last days, the letter says, Bede was translating the Gospel of John into English. He got as far as a verse in chapter six. A boy has a little food, and Andrew asks Jesus, "but what are they among so many?"
He also stopped to hand out a few small things he owned, a little pepper, some cloth, some incense, to the priests of the house. Then the boy, Wilberht, says it. Dear master, one sentence left.
A moment later: it's finished. And Bede answers, you've spoken truly, it is finished. They are the words Jesus says from the cross in John's Gospel.
Bede asks to be held, facing the place where he used to pray, and he dies on the floor of his cell, singing the old words of praise: glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.
A whole life of work, and the last sentence still mattered.

how: Catholics and Anglicans honor the Venerable Bede as a saint, and Catholics count him a Doctor of the Church; his history is still read by students of the early English church.

practice: Think of something small you left half-done: an email in versions, a thank-you note, a sentence you started saying to someone and swallowed.
Choose one, and if you can, finish it now; if it has to wait, settle the exact words in your head. If you pray, offer the small work to God; if not, simply let it be done.
